title: Given an array where each element is the maximum jump length, return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index (assume the end is always reachable).
shortTitle: Jump Game II — minimum jumps to reach the end (greedy BFS layers)

s1_definition.profdef: Greedy layered BFS: treat each jump as expanding a range. Maintain the current jump's far boundary and the farthest reachable overall; when the index reaches the current boundary, increment the jump count and move the boundary to the farthest. Time O(n), space O(1).
s1_definition.analogy: A courier at National Bank of India wants the fewest hops across stages. Within one hop he can land anywhere in a window; he scouts the whole window to find the farthest he could then reach, and only counts a new hop when he steps off the edge of the current window.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count a jump when i hits the current window end; extend the window to farthest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Greedy layered BFS: treat each jump as expanding a range. Maintain the current jump's far boundary and the farthest reachable overall; when the index reaches the current boundary, increment the jump count and move the boundary to the farthest. Time O(n), space O(1).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A courier at National Bank of India wants the fewest hops across stages. Within one hop he can land anywhere in a window; he scouts the whole window to find the farthest he could then reach, and only counts a new hop when he steps off the edge of the current window.

**One line to remember:** Count a jump when i hits the current window end; extend the window to farthest.

sections.s2_technical:
Keep three values: jumps counted, the current window's end boundary, and the farthest reachable. Walk i from zero to the second-to-last index (you never need to jump from the last index). At each step extend farthest to max(farthest, i + nums[i]). When i equals the current boundary, you have exhausted the current jump's range, so increment jumps and set the boundary to farthest. For example: `farthest = Math.max(farthest, i + nums[i]); if (i == end) { jumps++; end = farthest; }`.

This is breadth-first search expressed greedily: each jump is one BFS layer, and the boundary marks where the current layer ends. Because you always extend to the farthest reachable within a layer before incrementing, the count is minimal.

The time is O(n) and space is O(1). A senior nuance is why you iterate only to n−2: reaching or passing the last index inside the final window already counts the jump, so iterating to n−1 would overcount by one.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a courier crosses settlement stages and must use the fewest hops to reach the last stage, since each hop has a fixed handling cost. This is exactly how Jump Game II works.

Problem 2 — Minimizing hops is not the same as reaching the end; it needs layer-by-layer expansion. This is exactly why the greedy BFS boundary pattern is used.

The mini-project builds a `MinHopPlanner`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input jumps are two, three, one, one, four.

Step 1: At index zero farthest becomes two, and since index zero equals the window end zero, the first hop is counted and the window end moves to two.

Step 2: At index one farthest becomes four, at index two farthest stays four.

Step 3: At index two, when the index reaches the window end of two, the second hop is counted and the window end moves to four.

Step 4: The loop stops at the second-to-last index, so no further hop is counted.

Step 5: The minimum number of hops is two.

```text
2026-10-27T03:10:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Min Hop Planner (Jump Game II)
2026-10-27T03:10:00Z [INFO] Minimum jumps = 2
2026-10-27T03:10:00Z [INFO] {2,3,1,1,4} → 2
2026-10-27T03:10:00Z [INFO] Minimum jumps = 2
2026-10-27T03:10:00Z [INFO] {2,3,0,1,4} → 2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  jumps = 2 3 1 1 4
  i=0 far=2 ; i==end(0) → jumps=1, end=2
  i=1 far=4 ; i=2 far=4 ; i==end(2) → jumps=2, end=4
  stop at i=n-2 ; answer = 2   (each window = one BFS layer)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Jump Game II asks for the minimum number of jumps, and I solve it with a greedy layered breadth-first search expressed in constant space. I keep three things: the jump count, the far boundary of the current jump's window, and the farthest index reachable overall. As I walk the array I always extend the farthest reachable using the current index plus its jump.

The key moment is when the index reaches the current window's boundary. That means I have scouted the entire range of the current jump, so I increment the jump count and move the window boundary out to the farthest I found. Each window is one breadth-first layer, and because I always expand to the farthest reachable before counting a new jump, the count is minimal. I iterate only to the second-to-last index, because reaching the end inside the final window already counts that jump and going one further would overcount.

In my project at National Bank of India, a courier crossed settlement stages and had to use the fewest hops because each hop carried a fixed handling cost. Reaching the end is not the same as reaching it cheaply, so I used this greedy window expansion that gives the minimum number of hops in linear time.
